task.title: Phone app that signs in to a hosted Workbook board
task.description:
Workbook reaches a phone today only by pointing its browser at a `workbook serve` running on some computer, so the board is gone the moment that computer sleeps or leaves the network. This story is a phone app that signs in to a hosted Workbook board, the deployment described in "Hosted Workbook board for invited people who have no repository access", and works anywhere the phone has a connection.

The use case is the time away from the desk: check what is next, read a task, capture an idea as a new task, move something along, and have teammates and agents see that change the next time they sync. It serves a client PM who was invited to the board and a contributor alike. A solo developer who wants Workbook on their phone deploys the hosted board and invites themselves.

An earlier version of this story had the phone hold its own Git credentials and talk to the Git remote directly, with no server in between. That design is dropped. It could serve nobody without repository access, and it needed Git and the Workbook core rebuilt for a phone. Its text is in this task's history.

## How it works

- The app is given a hosted board's address, and the person signs in the way that deployment is configured, with the invite and account they already have. There is no separate phone account.
- The phone holds no Git credential and no copy of the repository. It reads and changes tasks through the server, which records each change as an ordinary Workbook operation under the signed-in person's email. A CLI or desktop user cannot tell a phone edit from a browser edit.
- The conflict rules stay in one place, on the server. The app sends what the person changed together with the version of the task they were looking at, so a concurrent edit to the same field surfaces as a conflict instead of one side vanishing.
- Revoking a person's account on the server ends their phone's access too.
- The app needs the server to be reachable. With no connection it opens to the last board it saw, and says plainly that it is offline and how old that board is.

## What makes this more than the board in a small window

- The board was not designed for a phone-sized screen: columns sit side by side, cards move by dragging, and the detail form assumes room.
- The interface between the board and the server was built for the board's own page, which always arrives from the server that answers it. An app installed from a store updates on its own schedule, so that interface needs a stated version, and the app has to say plainly when it and the server are too far apart.
- Sign-in on a phone goes through the phone's browser to whatever provider the deployment uses, and what comes back is kept in the platform's secure storage.
- If edits are accepted with no connection, they are visibly not yet sent until the server accepts them, and they are sent with the task version they were made against so a conflict is still caught.

## Decisions to settle before building

Settle these first and record the outcome on this task; each one that turns into real work becomes its own task depending on this one.

1. Whether the first version needs a native app at all, or the hosted board made to fit a phone screen and added to the home screen covers it. Proposed: make the hosted board fit a phone first, then judge what a native app would add.
2. Platform: iPhone, Android, or both, and which comes first.
3. Screens: native screens, or the hosted board shown inside the app.
4. Offline: a read-only last known board, or edits queued and sent when the connection returns.
5. First-version scope. Proposed: one or more hosted boards, the board and Next views, task detail, create, edit title, description, status, priority and labels, and assign to self. Proposed out: invites and accounts, status and priority vocabulary changes, conflict resolution beyond showing that one exists, and anything destructive.
6. Distribution: store listing or a test channel first, and where its release sits beside the CLI, desktop and hosted release lines.

## Done when

- With no computer of theirs running and the phone on cellular data, a person adds a hosted board by its address, signs in, sees the board, creates a task and changes another's status, and a teammate's next `workbook list` shows both under that person's email.
- An invited person with no access to any repository can do all of that, and the app never asks for a Git credential.
- In airplane mode the app opens, shows the last known board, and says it is offline. If decision 4 allows offline edits, an edit made then is marked not yet sent and is sent without help after the connection returns.
- An edit made on the phone and a different edit to the same field made from the CLI both survive as a visible conflict.
- After an admin revokes the person's account, the app can no longer read or change anything, and says why.
- An app too old or too new for the server it is pointed at says so, instead of failing in some other way.
- The README describes the phone as a client of the hosted board, with what works offline stated separately from what needs a connection.
